verses.zh: 耶和华说：以色列啊，你若回来归向我，若从我眼前除掉你可憎的偶像，你就不被迁移。
verses.en: “If you, Israel, want to come back,” says the Lord,“if you want to come back to me,[NOTE:1] you must get those disgusting idols[NOTE:2] out of my sightand must no longer go astray.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “If you, Israel, want to turn [away from your shameful ways (those described in 3:23-25)]…then you must turn back to me.” Or perhaps, “Israel, you must turn back…Yes, you must turn back to me.”
Heb “disgusting things.”
Or possibly, “If you get those disgusting idols out of my sight, you will not need to flee.” This is less probable because the normal meaning of the last verb is “to wander,” “to stray.”

verses.zh: 你必凭诚实、公平、公义，指着永生的耶和华起誓；列国必因耶和华称自己为有福，也必因他夸耀。
verses.en: You must be truthful, honest, and uprightwhen you take an oath saying, ‘As surely as the Lord lives!’[NOTE:1] If you do,[NOTE:2] the nations will pray to be as blessed by him as you areand will make him the object of their boasting.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “If you [= you must; see the translator’s note on the word “do” later in this verse] swear/take an oath, ‘As the Lord lives,’ in truth, justice, and righteousness…”

4:1-2a consists of a number of “if” clauses. Some are formally introduced by the Hebrew particle אִם (ʾim), while others are introduced by the conjunction “and.” Another conjunction (“and” = “then”) with a perfect in 4:2b introduces the consequence. The translation “You must…. If you do,” was chosen to avoid a long and complicated sentence.
Heb “bless themselves in him and make their boasts in him.”

verses.zh: 耶和华对犹大和耶路撒冷人如此说：要开垦你们的荒地，不要撒种在荆棘中。
verses.en: Yes,[NOTE:1] this is what the Lord has said to the people of Judah and Jerusalem: “Break up your unplowed ground, do not cast seeds among thorns.[NOTE:2]
notes: The particle כִּי (ki) is asseverative (“indeed, yes”) here rather than causal (“for”) because the content of v. 3 and following reaffirms the content of vv. 1-2.

The agricultural imagery seems to be that they are to plow over the thorns and make the ground ready for seeds that will produce a new crop. The spiritual application of breaking up their rebellious will and turning from sin is metaphorically stated in the next verse.

verses.zh: 犹大人和耶路撒冷的居民哪，你们当自行割礼，归耶和华，将心里的污秽除掉；恐怕我的忿怒因你们的恶行发作，如火着起，甚至无人能以熄灭！
verses.en: Commit yourselves to the Lord;dedicate your hearts to me[NOTE:1] people of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem.Otherwise, my anger will blaze up like a flaming fire against youthat no one will be able to extinguish.That will happen because of the evil you have done.”
notes: Heb “Circumcise yourselves to the Lord and remove the foreskin of your heart.” sn Circumcising the heart is a metaphor for being dedicated to the Lord. It is associated with not being stubborn and with loving God in Deut 10:16; 30:6. See also Josh 5 for a ceremony of circumcision connected with national dedication.

verses.zh: 你们当传扬在犹大，宣告在耶路撒冷说：你们当在国中吹角，高声呼叫说：你们当聚集！我们好进入坚固城！
verses.en: The Lord said,[NOTE:1] “Announce[NOTE:2] this in Judah and proclaim it in Jerusalem:[NOTE:3] ‘Sound the trumpet[NOTE:4] throughout the land!’Shout out loudly,‘Gather together! Let us flee into the fortified cities!’
notes: The words “The Lord said” are not in the text, but it is obvious from v. 6 and v. 9 that he is the speaker. These words are supplied in the translation for clarity.

It is unclear who the addressees of the masculine plural imperatives are here. They may be the citizens of Jerusalem and Judah who are sounding the alarm to others. However, the first person reference to the Lord in v. 6 and Jeremiah’s response in v. 10 suggest that this is a word from the Lord that he is commanded to pass on to the citizens of Jerusalem and Judah. If the imperatives are not merely rhetorical plurals, they may reflect the practice referred to in Jer 23:18, 22; Amos 3:7. A similar phenomenon also occurs in Jer 5:1 and Isa 40:1-2. This may also be the explanation for the plural imperatives in Jer 31:6. For further discussion see the translator’s note on Jer 5:1.
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Heb “ram’s horn.” But the modern equivalent is “trumpet” and is more readily understandable.

verses.zh: 应当向锡安竖立大旗。要逃避，不要迟延，因我必使灾祸与大毁灭从北方来到。
verses.en: Raise a signal flag that tells people to go to Zion.[NOTE:1] Run for safety! Do not delay!For I am about to bring disaster out of the north.It will bring great destruction.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Raise up a signal toward Zion.”
Heb “out of the north, even great destruction.”

verses.zh: 有狮子从密林中上来，是毁坏列国的。它已经动身出离本处，要使你的地荒凉，使你的城邑变为荒场无人居住。
verses.en: Like a lion that has come up from its lair,[NOTE:1] the one who destroys nations has set out from his home base.[NOTE:2] He is coming out to lay your land waste.Your cities will become ruins and lie uninhabited.
notes: Heb “A lion has left its lair.” The metaphor is turned into a simile for clarification. The word translated “lair” has also been understood to refer to a hiding place. However, it appears to be cognate in meaning to the word translated “lair” in Ps 10:9; Jer 25:38, a word which also refers to the abode of the Lord in Ps 76:3.
Heb “his place.”

verses.zh: 因此，你们当腰束麻布，大声哀号，因为耶和华的烈怒没有向我们转消。
verses.en: So put on sackcloth!Mourn and wail, saying,‘The fierce anger of the Lordhas not turned away from us!’[NOTE:1]
notes: Or “wail because the fierce anger of the Lord has not turned away from us.” The translation does not need to assume a shift in speaker as the alternate reading does.

verses.zh: 耶和华说：「到那时，君王和首领的心都要消灭；祭司都要惊奇，先知都要诧异。」
verses.en: When this happens,”[NOTE:1] says the Lord,“the king and his officials will lose their courage.The priests will be struck with horror,and the prophets will be speechless in astonishment.”
notes: Heb “In that day.”

verses.zh: 我说：「哀哉！主耶和华啊，你真是大大地欺哄这百姓和耶路撒冷，说：『你们必得平安』。其实刀剑害及性命了。」
verses.en: In response to all this[NOTE:1] I said, “Ah, Sovereign Lord,[NOTE:2] you have surely allowed[NOTE:3] the people of Judah and Jerusalem[NOTE:4] to be deceived by those who say, ‘You will be safe!’[NOTE:5] But in fact a sword is already at our throats.”[NOTE:6]
notes: The words “In response to all this” are not in the text but are supplied in the translation to clarify the connection.
Heb “Lord Yahweh.” The translation follows the ancient Jewish tradition of substituting the Hebrew word for God for the proper name Yahweh.

Or “You have deceived.” The Hiphil of נָשָׁא (nashaʾ, “to deceive”) is understood in a tolerative sense here: “to allow [someone] to be deceived.” IBHS 446 §27.5c, notes that this function of the Hiphil describes caused activity that is “welcome to the undersubject, but unacceptable or disagreeable to a third party.” Jerusalem and Judah welcomed the assurances of false prophets who deceived them. Although this was detestable to God, he allowed it.
Heb “this people and Jerusalem.”

Heb “Jerusalem, saying, ‘You will have peace’”; or “You have deceived the people of Judah and Jerusalem, saying, ‘You will have peace.’” The words “you will be safe” are, of course, those of the false prophets (cf., Jer 6:14; 8:11; 14:13; 23:16-17). It is difficult to tell whether the charge here is meant literally as the emotional outburst of the prophet (compare for example, Jer 15:18) or whether it is to be understood as a figure of speech in which a verb of direct causation is to be understood as permissive or tolerative, i.e., God did not command the prophets to say this but allowed them to do so. While it is not beyond God to use false prophets to accomplish his will (cf., e.g., 1 Kgs 22:19-23), he elsewhere in the book of Jeremiah directly denies having sent the false prophets to say such things as this (cf., e.g., Jer 14:14-15; 23:21, 32). For examples of the use of this figure of speech, see E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech, 571, 823 and compare Ezek 20:25. The translation given attempts to resolve the issue.
Heb “touches the throat/soul.” For this use of the word usually translated “soul” or “life,” see HALOT 672 s.v. נֶפֶשׁ 1-2, and compare the use in Ps 105:18.

verses.zh: 那时，必有话对这百姓和耶路撒冷说：「有一阵热风从旷野净光的高处向我的众民（原文是民女）刮来，不是为簸扬，也不是为扬净。
verses.en: At that time the people of Judah and Jerusalem[NOTE:1] will be told,“A scorching wind will sweep downfrom the hilltops in the wilderness on[NOTE:2] my dear people.[NOTE:3] It will not be a gentle breezefor winnowing[NOTE:4] the grain and blowing away the chaff.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “this people and Jerusalem.”

Heb “A scorching wind from the hilltops in the desert toward…”sn The allusion is, of course, to the destructive forces of the enemy armies of Babylon, compared above in 4:7 to a destructive lion and here to the destructive desert winds of the Near Eastern sirocco.

Heb “daughter of my people.” The term “daughter of” is appositional to “my people” and is supplied in the translation as a term of sympathy and endearment. Compare the common expression “daughter of Zion.”

Heb “not for winnowing and not for cleansing.” The words “It will not be a gentle breeze” are not in the text but are implicit in the connection. They are supplied in the translation here for clarification.
The word “No” is not in the text but is carried over from the connection with the preceding line “not for…”

verses.zh: 必有一阵更大的风从这些地方为我刮来；现在我又必发出判语，攻击他们。」
verses.en: No,[NOTE:1] a wind too strong for that will come at my bidding.Yes, even now I, myself, am calling down judgment on them.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “will speak judgments against them.”

Heb “he is coming up like clouds.” The words “The enemy” are supplied in the translation to identify the referent, and the word “gathering” is supplied to try to convey the significance of the simile, i.e., that of quantity and of an approaching storm.

verses.zh: 看哪，仇敌必如云上来；他的战车如旋风，他的马匹比鹰更快。我们有祸了！我们败落了！
verses.en: Look! The enemy is approaching like gathering clouds.[NOTE:1] The roar of his chariots is like that of a whirlwind.[NOTE:2] His horses move more swiftly than eagles.”I cry out,[NOTE:3] “We are doomed,[NOTE:4] for we will be destroyed!”
notes: Heb “his chariots [are] like a whirlwind.” The words “roar” and “sound” are supplied in the translation to clarify the significance of the simile.

The words “I cry out” are not in the text, but the words that follow are obviously not the Lord’s. They are either those of the people or of Jeremiah. Taking them as Jeremiah’s parallels the interjection of Jeremiah’s response in 4:10 that is formally introduced.

Heb “Woe to us!” The words “woe to” are common in funeral laments and at the beginning of oracles of judgment. In many contexts they carry the connotation of hopelessness or apprehensiveness of inevitable doom.
Heb “O, Jerusalem, wash your heart from evil.”

verses.zh: 耶路撒冷啊，你当洗去心中的恶，使你可以得救。恶念存在你心里要到几时呢？
verses.en: O people of Jerusalem, purify your hearts from evil[NOTE:1] so that you may yet be delivered.How long will you continue to harbor upwicked schemes within you?
notes: Heb “For a voice declaring from Dan and making heard disaster from the hills of Ephraim.”

verses.zh: 有声音从但传扬，从以法莲山报祸患。
verses.en: For messengers are coming, heralding disaster,from the city of Dan and from the hills of Ephraim.[NOTE:1]
notes: The words “They are saying” are not in the text but are implicit in the connection and are supplied in the translation for clarification.

verses.zh: 你们当传给列国，报告攻击耶路撒冷的事说：有探望的人从远方来到，向犹大的城邑大声呐喊。
verses.en: They are saying,[NOTE:1] “Announce to the surrounding nations,[NOTE:2] ‘The enemy is coming!’[NOTE:3] Proclaim this message[NOTE:4] to Jerusalem:‘Those who besiege cities[NOTE:5] are coming from a distant land.They are ready to raise the battle cry against[NOTE:6] the towns in Judah.’
notes: The word “surrounding” is not in the text but is implicit and is supplied in the translation for clarification.

Or “Here they come!” Heb “Look!” or “Behold!” Or “Announce to the surrounding nations, indeed [or yes], proclaim to Jerusalem, ‘Besiegers…’” The text is very elliptical here. Some of the modern English versions appear to be emending the text from הִנֵּה (hinneh, “behold”) to either הֵנָּה (hennah, “these things”; so NEB), or הַזֶּה (hazzeh, “this”; so NIV). The solution proposed here is as old as the LXX, which reads, “Behold, they have come.”
The words, “this message,” are not in the text but are supplied in the translation to make the introduction of the quote easier.
Heb “Besiegers.” For the use of this verb to refer to besieging a city, compare Isa 1:8.
Heb “They have raised their voices against.” The verb here, a vav (ו) consecutive with an imperfect, continues the nuance of the preceding participle “are coming.”

Heb “will surround her.” The antecedent is Jerusalem in the preceding verse. The referent is again made explicit in the translation to avoid any possible lack of clarity. The verb form here emphasizes the fact as being as good as done (i.e., it is a prophetic perfect).

verses.zh: 他们周围攻击耶路撒冷，好像看守田园的，因为她背叛了我。这是耶和华说的。
verses.en: They will surround Jerusalem[NOTE:1] like men guarding a field[NOTE:2] because they have rebelled against me,”says the Lord.
notes: There is some irony involved in the choice of the simile since the men guarding a field were there to keep thieves from getting in and stealing the crops. Here the besiegers are guarding the city to keep people from getting out.
Heb “Your way and your deeds.”

verses.zh: 你的行动，你的作为，招惹这事；这是你罪恶的结果，实在是苦，是害及你心了！
verses.en: “The way you have lived and the things you have done[NOTE:1] will bring this on you.This is the punishment you deserve, and it will be painful indeed.[NOTE:2] The pain will be so bad it will pierce your heart.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “How bitter!”

Heb “Indeed, it reaches to your heart.” The subject must be the pain alluded to in the last half of the preceding line; the verb is masculine, agreeing with the adjective translated “painful.” The only other possible antecedent, “punishment,” is feminine.
The words “I said” are not in the text. They are used to mark the shift from the Lord’s promise of judgment to Jeremiah’s lament concerning it.

verses.zh: 我的肺腑啊，我的肺腑啊，我心疼痛！我心在我里面烦躁不安。我不能静默不言，因为我已经听见角声和打仗的喊声。
verses.en: I said,[NOTE:1] “Oh, the feeling in the pit of my stomach![NOTE:2] I writhe in anguish.Oh, the pain in my heart![NOTE:3] My heart pounds within me.I cannot keep silent.For I hear the sound of the trumpet;[NOTE:4] the sound of the battle cry pierces my soul![NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “My bowels! My bowels!”
Heb “the walls of my heart!”
Heb “ram’s horn.” But the modern equivalent is “trumpet” and is more readily understandable.

The translation reflects a different division of the last two lines than that suggested by the Masoretes. The written text (the Kethib) reads “for the sound of the ram’s horn I have heard [or “you have heard,” if the form is understood as the old second feminine singular perfect] my soul” followed by “the battle cry” in the last line. The translation is based on taking “my soul” with the last line and understanding an elliptical expression “[to] my soul the battle cry.” Such an elliptical expression is in keeping with the elliptical nature of the exclamations at the beginning of the verse (cf. the literal translations of the first two lines of the verse in the notes on the words “stomach” and “heart”).

The words “I see” are not in the text here or at the beginning of the third line. They are supplied in the translation to show that this is Jeremiah’s vision of what will happen as a result of the invasion announced in 4:5-9, 11-17a.

verses.zh: 毁坏的信息连络不绝，因为全地荒废。我的帐棚忽然毁坏；我的幔子顷刻破裂。
verses.en: I see[NOTE:1] one destruction after another taking place,so that the whole land lies in ruins.I see our[NOTE:2] tents suddenly destroyed,their[NOTE:3] curtains torn down in a mere instant.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “my.” This is probably not a reference to Jeremiah’s own tents since he foresees the destruction of the whole land. Jeremiah so identifies with the plight of his people that he sees the destruction of their tents as though they were his very own. It would probably lead to confusion to translate literally, and it is not uncommon in Hebrew laments for the community or its representative to speak of the community as an “I.” See, for example, the interchange between first singular and first plural pronouns in Ps 44:4-8.
Heb “my.”

It is not altogether clear what Jeremiah intends by the use of this metaphor. In all likelihood he means that the defenses of Israel’s cities and towns have offered no more resistance than nomads’ tents. However, in light of the fact that the word “tent” came to be used generically for a person’s home (cf. 1 Kgs 8:66; 12:16), it is possible here that Jeremiah is referring to the destruction of their homes and the resultant feeling of homelessness and loss of even elementary protection. Given the lack of certainty, the present translation is rather literal here.
Heb “the sound of ram’s horns.” But the modern equivalent is “bugles” and is more readily understandable.

verses.zh: 我看见大旗，听见角声，要到几时呢？
verses.en: How long must I see the enemy’s battle flagsand hear the military signals of their bugles?”[NOTE:1]
notes: These words are not in the text but are supplied in the translation to show clearly the shift in speaker. Jeremiah has been speaking; now the Lord answers, giving the reason for the devastation Jeremiah foresees.

verses.zh: 耶和华说：我的百姓愚顽，不认识我；他们是愚昧无知的儿女，有智慧行恶，没有知识行善。
verses.en: The Lord answered,[NOTE:1] “This will happen[NOTE:2] because my people are foolish.They do not know me.They are like children who have no sense.[NOTE:3] They have no understanding.They are skilled at doing evil.They do not know how to do good.”
notes: Heb “For….” This gives the explanation for the destruction envisaged in 4:20 to which Jeremiah responds in 4:19, 21.
Heb “They are senseless children.”
Heb “I looked at the land and behold…” This indicates the visionary character of Jeremiah’s description of the future condition of the land of Israel.

verses.zh: 先知说：我观看地，不料，地是空虚混沌；我观看天，天也无光。
verses.en: I looked at the land and saw[NOTE:1] that it was an empty wasteland.[NOTE:2] I looked up at the sky, and its light had vanished.
notes: Heb “formless and empty.” This is a case of hendiadys (two nouns joined by “and” both describe the same thing): one noun retains its full nominal force; the other functions as an adjective. The words תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ (tohu vavohu) allude to Gen 1:2, hyperbolically picturing a reversal of creation and return to the original precreation chaos.
Heb “there was no man/human being.”

verses.zh: 我观看大山，不料，尽都震动，小山也都摇来摇去。
verses.en: I looked at the mountains and saw that they were shaking.All the hills were swaying back and forth!

verses.zh: 我观看，不料，无人；空中的飞鸟也都躲避。
verses.en: I looked and saw that there were no more people[NOTE:1] and that all the birds in the sky had flown away.
notes: Heb “because of the Lord, because of his blazing anger.”

verses.zh: 我观看，不料，肥田变为荒地；一切城邑在耶和华面前，因他的烈怒都被拆毁。
verses.en: I looked and saw that the fruitful land had become a desertand that all the cities had been laid in ruins.The Lord had brought this all aboutbecause of his blazing anger.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “For this is what the Lord said.”

verses.zh: 耶和华如此说：全地必然荒凉，我却不毁灭净尽。
verses.en: All this will happen because the Lord said,[NOTE:1] “The whole land will be desolate;however, I will not completely destroy it.
notes: The earth and the heavens are personified here and depicted in the act of mourning and wearing black clothes because of the destruction of the land of Israel.

verses.zh: 因此，地要悲哀，在上的天也必黑暗；因为我言已出，我意已定，必不后悔，也不转意不做。
verses.en: Because of this, the land will mournand the sky above will grow black.[NOTE:1] For I have made my purpose known,[NOTE:2] and I will not relent or turn back from carrying it out.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “has spoken and purposed.” This is an example of hendiadys where two verbs are joined by “and” but one is meant to serve as a modifier of the other.
Heb “will not turn back from it.”

Heb “And you that are doomed to destruction.” The referent is supplied from the following context and the fact that Zion/Jerusalem represents the leadership that was continually making overtures to foreign nations for help.

verses.zh: 各城的人因马兵和弓箭手的响声就都逃跑，进入密林，爬上磐石；各城被撇下，无人住在其中。
verses.en: At the sound of the approaching horsemen and archersthe people of every town will flee.Some of them will hide in the thickets.Others will climb up among the rocks.All the cities will be deserted.No one will remain in them.

verses.zh: 你凄凉的时候要怎样行呢？你虽穿上朱红衣服，佩戴黄金装饰，用颜料修饰眼目，这样标致是枉然的！恋爱你的藐视你，并且寻索你的性命。
verses.en: And you, Zion, city doomed to destruction,[NOTE:1] you accomplish nothing[NOTE:2] by wearing a beautiful dress,[NOTE:3] decking yourself out in jewels of gold,and putting on eye shadow![NOTE:4] You are making yourself beautiful for nothing.Your lovers spurn you.They want to kill you.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “What are you accomplishing…?” The rhetorical question assumes a negative answer, made clear by the translation in the indicative.
Heb “clothing yourself in scarlet.”
Heb “enlarging your eyes with antimony.” Antimony was a black powder used by women as eyeliner to make their eyes look larger.
Heb “they seek your life.”
The particle כִּי (ki) is more likely asseverative here than causal.

verses.zh: 我听见有声音，彷佛妇人产难的声音，好像生头胎疼痛的声音，是锡安女子（就是指民的意思）的声音；她喘着气、挓挲手，说：我有祸了！在杀人的跟前，我的心发昏了。
verses.en: In fact,[NOTE:1] I hear a cry like that of a woman in labor,a cry of anguish like that of a woman giving birth to her first baby.It is the cry of Daughter Zion[NOTE:2] gasping for breath,reaching out for help,[NOTE:3] saying, “I am done in![NOTE:4] My life is ebbing away before these murderers!”
notes: Jerusalem is personified as a helpless young woman giving birth.
Heb “spreading out her hands.” The idea of asking or pleading for help is implicit in the figure.
Heb “Woe, now to me!” See the translator’s note on 4:13 for the usage of “Woe to…”

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- This chapter is a series of poems on different subjects. Verses 5-31 contain several
independant poems about Judah's invasion.

- Jeremiah 4:1-2 describe repentance and relate to Jeremiah 3, Jer. 4:21-25.

- The theme of Judah's rebellion and YHWH's judgment by foreign invasion runs through Jeremiah 6.

- Notice the number of ways the God-sent invaders are described

- the lion, v. 7

- the destroyer, v. 7

- he. . ., v. 13

- besiegers, v. 16

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: JEREMIAH 4:1-2

1"If you will return, O Israel," declares the Lord,

"Then you should return to Me.

And if you will put away your detested things from My presence,

And will not waver,

2And you will swear, 'As the Lord lives,'

In truth, in justice and in righteousness;

Then the nations will bless themselves in Him,

And in Him they will glory."

4:1 "If" Grammatically there seem to be four "ifs" or conditions in Jer. 4:1-2. This shows the
conditional nature of the covenant (i.e. "if. . .then. . .," cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-28; also
note Deut. 30:15,19; Psalm 1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "return. . .return to Me" The Hebrew root, שׁוב (BDB 996-1000), is used
in several words, in several lines in chapters 3:1-4:2.

- שׁוב ‒ "return," Jer. 3:1 (twice), 7 (twice), 10,12,14,19,22; 4:1 (twice)

‒ "turn away," Jer. 4:8

‒ "turn back," Jer. 4:28

- שׁובב (BDB 1000) ‒ "faithless," Jer. 3:14,22

- משׁובה, (BDB 1000) ‒ "faithless," Jer. 3:6,11,12

‒ "backsliding," 3:22

Notice the personal emphasis (cf. Jer. 3:1,4,7,10,19,20). Sin is more than a violation of
a law code. It is a personal affront to a personal God (i.e. Gen. 20:6; 39:9; 2 Sam. 12:13; Ps. 41:4; 51:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

▣ Notice the list of things YHWH asks His wayward, faithless, covenant people to do.

- return (twice, meaning to repent, that is turn from idols and turn to YHWH)

- put away (BDB 693, KB 747, Hiphil IMPERFECT) your idols (cf. Jer. 7:17-18)

- do not waver, that whole hearted repentance, not half-heart pretending

- you will swear "as the Lord lives," which is a faith and commitment oath, cf. Deut. 6:13; 10:20; Jer. 12:16)

▣ "Israel" This title (BDB 975, KB 442) can mean

- a new name given to Jacob

- a collective term for all the children of Jacob

- the northern ten tribes after the split of the United Monarchy in 922 B.C. They
were later taken captive by Assyria at the fall of the capital, Samaria in 722 B.C.

Context must determine which meaning. This is especially hard in Jeremiah when #2 and #3 are
used in isolated poems without their historical setting specified.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

▣ "detested things" This is literally "abominations" (BDB 1055) and refers to idols.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

▣ "and will not waver" This VERB (BDB 626, KB 678, Qal
IMPERFECT, lit. "wander," cf. Gen. 4:12,14) refers to wholehearted daily activities
(i.e. lifestyle).

King David had a whole hearted devotion to YHWH (cf. 1 Kgs. 3:14; 9:4), but his son,
Solomon, had only half hearted devotion to YHWH (cf. 1 Kgs. 11:2,4,9). Idolatry destroys faith, trust, and
dependence on YHWH and YHWH alone!

4:2 "you will swear" This VERB (BDB 989, KB 1396, Niphal PERFECT with
waw) refers to a verbal act of worship, much like our modern liturgies (cf. Jer. 12:16; Deut. 6:13;
10:20; Isa. 65:16). Idolaters swear by Ba'al, but YHWH's people swear allegiance only to Him! This is
theologically parallel to Rom. 10:9-13, which is a quote from Joel 2:32 (cf. Acts 2:21).

▣ "In truth, in justice and in righteousness" This is the attitude of "swear." It refers to
a lifestyle response, not only a ritual or periodic emotional experiences. This would describe true repentance. Each
of these three words carries theological meaning.

- in truth (BDB 54, see Special Topic below)

- in justice (BDB 1048, see Special Topic below)

- in righteousness (BDB 842, see Special Topic below)

SPECIAL TOPIC: AMEN

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDGE, JUDGMENT, and JUSTICE IN ISAIAH

SPECIAL
TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣ "the nations will bless themselves in Him" This is a recurrent theme in Genesis (BDB 138,
KB 159, Hithpael PERFECT with waw, cf. Gen. 12:3; 18:18; 22:18; 26:41; 28:14). God's promises
to the Patriarchs show Israel's purpose as an instrument of reaching the whole world (cf. Exod. 19:5-6; Isa. 42:6; 49:6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN)

This is such an important theological concept that I have included my notes from Gen. 12:3.

The Niphal stem is usually PASSIVE (LXX, NASB, "shall be blessed,"
cf. Jer. 18:18; 28:14), but in Jer. 22:18 and 26:4 the Hithpael PERFECT stem is used, which is
REFLEXIVE ("bless themselves"). It is possible that the Hithpael denotes
a continuing action through time. It is significant that God includes all nations in His promise
to Abram in light of the universal rebellion of chapter 11. God chose Abraham to choose all
humans made in His image (cf. Ps. 22:27; 66:4; 86:9; Isa. 25:6-12; 56:6-8; 60:1-3; 66:23; Acts 3:25; Gal. 3:8)! Also
see note at Gen. 22:18.

This is really an important passage. It shows clearly God's purpose of using
Abram to reach all the world. The universal promise of Gen. 3:15 is being implemented, even amidst
the purposeful rebellion of Noah's children (i.e. Genesis 10 and 11). It s not only to those who
show favor to Abram, but to those who will show favor to Abram's seed (i.e. the Messiah). There
was/is a universal purpose in YHWH's choice of "one" to bring prophesied redemption through the
special "One" of his descendants. In the big picture, this is not a text about an attitude toward Jews,
but a faith response to the Jewish "promised One."

▣ "in Him they will glory" The VERB (BDB 237, KB 248) is Hithpael
IMPERFECT, denoting ongoing action. Followers of YHWH glory/boast in knowing Him and
Him alone (cf. Jer. 9:23-24). Notice the wonderful, universal implications of Isa. 45:20-25, especially
Jer. 4:25b! Biblical faith is a personal relationship with the one true God!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL FAITH IS CORPORATE

▣ "Break up your fallow ground" Verse 3 relates to the agricultural practice of preparing

dwell on becomes who we are!

Repentance is plowed, good ground, ready for fellowship and obedience in a daily walk
with God.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: JEREMIAH 4:5-9

5Declare in Judah and proclaim in Jerusalem, and say,

"Blow the trumpet in the land;

Cry aloud and say,

'Assemble yourselves, and let us go

Into the fortified cities.'

6Lift up a standard toward Zion!

Seek refuge, do not stand still,

For I am bringing evil from the north,

And great destruction.

7A lion has gone up from his thicket,

And a destroyer of nations has set out;

He has gone out from his place

To make your land a waste.

Your cities will be ruins

Without inhabitant.

8For this, put on sackcloth,

Lament and wail;

For the fierce anger of the Lord

Has not turned back from us.

9It shall come about in that day," declares the Lord,
"that the heart of the king and the heart of the princes will fail; and the priests will be appalled and the prophets will be astounded."

4:5 "Blow the trumpet" This is the word shophar. It was used as a call to war or for
religious observances. Jer. 4:5-9 forms a poem of a watchman.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORNS USED BY ISRAEL

▣ "in the land" This is the Hebrew term erets (BDB 75, KB 90). It has a wide semantic field.
It is obvious from this context that it means Judah.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH

▣ "Into the fortified cities" When an enemy approached, all the people of the surrounding unwalled villages
rushed to the nearest city with a protective wall (i.e. Jer. 8:14).

4:6 "Lift up a standard" A standard (BDB 651) serves several purposes.

- a call to assemble

- a call to gather for war ‒ Isa. 5:26; 13:2; 18:3-4; Jer. 50:2; 51:12

- a call to rush to a walled city ‒ Jer. 4:6,21

- a call for Gentiles to come to YHWH in peace ‒ Isa. 11:10; 18:3; 49:22; 62:10

- YHWH is a banner for His people ‒ Exod. 17:15

▣ "Zion" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ZION.

▣ "evil from the north" The "north" was a symbol of evil because it was the route of invasion for the
Mesopotamian powers (i.e. Assyria, Babylon, Persia, cf. Jer. 1:14,15; 6:1,22; 10:22; 50:3; Isa. 41:25). Although, some
see it as the invasion of the Scythians, according to Herodotus.

4:7 "lion" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

▣ "a destroyer of nations has set out" This is literally "struck his tents." It refers to
Nebuchadnezzar II of Neo-Babylon, who took Judah into exile in 605, 597, 586, 582 B.C.,
as Assyria did Israel in 722 B.C.

4:8 "put on sackcloth" See SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES.

▣ "the fierce anger of the Lord has not turned back from us" This is a play on the
phrase "turn back" (BDB 996, KB 1427), which is also the term for "repentance," cf. v. 1 (twice). YHWH will not relent of His
wrath on His covenant people for their idolatry.

4:9 "in that day" This phrase was a way of referring to the special future day of YHWH's
visitation (cf. Jer. 4:11a). It can be for blessing or judgment, here judgment.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

▣ "the king. . .the princes. . .the priests. . .the prophets" This refers to those leaders
who rejected Jeremiah's message (cf. Jer. 1:18; 2:8,26; 5:31; 6:13; 8:1,10; 13:13; 14:18; 23:33-34). Judah
had no godly leaders!

▣ Notice the parallel VERBS.

- fail ‒ BDB 1, KB 2, Qal IMPERFECT

- appalled ‒ BDB 1030, KB 1563, Niphal PERFECT with waw (related
form "waste" in Jer. 4:7)

- astounded ‒ BDB 1069, KB 1744, Qal IMPERFECT (found only here
in Jeremiah)

The leadership (civil and religious) will utterly fail and not know what to do in light of
the invasion. Their eyes have been blinded by idolatry and false prophets (cf. Jer. 4:10); they cannot
find YHWH! Therefore, the common proverb has come true—"As the leaders go, so go the people!"

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: JEREMIAH 4:10

10Then I said, "Ah, Lord God! Surely You have
utterly deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, 'You will have peace'; whereas a sword touches the throat."

4:10 "Then I said" Who is speaking?

- the prophet (Jeremiah)

- the people of Judah

- false prophets (i.e. you will have "peace")

The MT has "Then I said," but the LXX has, "And they shall say."

See my comment in the next item.

▣ "Surely You have utterly deceived this people" Jer. 4:10 is a comment from Jeremiah to YHWH
about the message of the false prophets. Jeremiah speaks bluntly and honestly to God (cf. Jer. 12:1;
15:17-18; 20:7-9). This false message of hope and deliverance from invasion was what the false prophets
were preaching in God's name (cf. Jer. 6:14; 8:11; 14:13; 23:16-17; 28:1ff). God let this occur but both the
speaker and hearer are responsible!

The MT has the Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and the Hiphil
PERFECT VERB, which was a grammatical way to denote emphasis ("utterly deceived").

One more possibility in understanding this difficult phrase is that the people were
clinging to Isaiah's prophecies about the invulnerability of Jerusalem (cf. Isaiah 36-39). Jeremiah
would have to remind them that Isaiah's promises were also based on a conditional covenant model
(i.e. "if. . .then. . .," cf. Jer. 4:1-2). Judah did not obey the covenant, therefore, its curses,
not its promises, were what they would reap (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28-29).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "peace" See SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE (OT).

▣ "throat" This is the word nephesh (BDB 659, cf. Gen. 2:7 [of man] and 2:19 [of animals]). It basically
means the life on this planet that breathes (related to the Hebrew word for "breath").

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

11In that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem, "A scorching wind
from the bare heights in the wilderness in the direction of the daughter of My people-not to winnow and not to cleanse, 12a

13Behold, he goes up like clouds,

And his chariots like the whirlwind;

4:11 "A scorching wind" This refers to the sirocco desert winds, often used in the OT as
imagery for judgment (i.e. "not to winnow, and not to cleanse," cf. Jer. 4:12).

▣ "from the bare heights" This was the physical locality of Ba'al worship
(cf. Jer. 2:20; 3:2,6; 4:11; 7:29; 14:6; 17:2; Isa. 57:7; Deut. 12:2). It was also the place where winnowing occurred.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "the daughter of My people" See notes at Jer. 46:11.

▣ "not to winnow" The wind will be too strong and too hot for harvesting grain. The last
item, "cleanse," probably refers to the process of separating the husk from the grain (DSS).

The implication is that husk and grain (i.e. the faithful and the unfaithful) will both be destroyed.

4:12 "at My command" God sent these judgments; they were carried out by Mesopotamian pagan
nations! There are consequences to covenant disobedience (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28-29)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

4:13 This is imagery for God's judgment (i.e. lines a-c refer to the invaders, "he," cf. v. 7) and the results.

- woe to us (BDB 17, cf. Jer. 4:31; 6:4; 10:19; 13:27)

- we are ruined (BDB 994, KB 1418, Pual PERFECT, same VERB
found in Jer. 4:20; 9:19; 10:20; 48:1,15,20; 49:3,10)

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: JEREMIAH 4:14-18

14"Wash your heart from evil, O Jerusalem,

That you may be saved.

How long will your wicked thoughts

Lodge within you?

15For a voice declares from Dan,

And proclaims wickedness from Mount Ephraim.

16Report it to the nations, now!

Proclaim over Jerusalem,

'Besiegers come from a far country,

4:14 "Wash your heart" This VERB (BDB 460, KB 459, Piel IMPERATIVE)
is an allusion to washing a soiled garment, which is imagery for repentance and cleansing
(cf. Ps. 51:2,7; Isa. 1:16; Jer. 2:2). It is a call, like Ezekiel 18, for an individual to turn back to YHWH
and change his ways (cf. Jer. 4:3-4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

▣ "That you may be saved" The Hebrew VERB (BDB 446, KB 448, Niphal
IMPERFECT) has two connotations.

- physical deliverance

- spiritual forgiveness

Both are needed for Judah to avert YHWH's coming judgment!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT term)

▣ "wicked thoughts" Maybe this is best illustrated by Jer. 13:27.

4:15 "voice. . .from Dan" This was the farthest northern tribe in Palestine. The tribe of Dan, in
unbelief, moved from its tribal allocation in the south (i.e. because of the Philistine occupation of their tribal
inheritance, cf. Josh. 19:40-48) to the north (cf. Judges 18).

The phrase "from Dan to Beersheba" became a way to denote the whole Promised Land (cf. Jdg. 20:1;
1 Sam. 3:20; 2 Sam. 3:10; 17:11; 24:2; 2 Chr. 30:5; Amos 8:14).

▣ "Mount Ephraim" This refers to the central mountainous (i.e. hill country) region of
Palestine, which was the tribal allocation of Ephraim (cf. Josh. 17:15; 19:50; 20:7). The mountains of
Ebal and Gerizim (i.e. Samaria) were in this region.

Dan and Ephraim fell to the Assyrians in 722 B.C. Now that destruction
would come to Judah and Jerusalem (cf. Jer. 4:16-17) and the northern invaders were close!

4:16 This verse starts with two commands to make known YHWH's coming judgment to Judah.

- report ‒ BDB 269, KB 269, Hiphil IMPERATIVE (this could refer to
the mercenary invaders, Jer. 4:16c)

- proclaim ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

The voice from Dan (Jer. 4:15)

- tells the invaders (or the surrounding nations to Judah) they are close to Jerusalem

- tells Jerusalem that the invaders are close to them!

▣ "Besiegers come from a far country" The VERBAL (BDB 665, KB 718, Qal
ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) in this context has the meaning of "besiege" (BDB 666, #5, cf. Isa. 1:8;
Ezek. 6:12). It usually is translated "enemies."

- The UBS Handbook (p. 133) suggests advanced scouts of the Neo- Babylonian army.

- The UBS Text Project, p. 184, suggests it refers to enemy guards who watched besieged cities for those trying to escape.

4:17 "Like watchmen of a field" I must admit that I do not understand this phrase in this context. TEV
takes it to mean watchmen that surround a field ready to harvest. But here they guard against any persons
escaping the besieged city (NET Bible, footnote, #13).

The UBS Handbook (p. 134) suggests that the imagery is connected to the "tents"
(booths) of the agricultural watchmen, but here with the army tents of the invaders (v. 7).

▣ "Because she has rebelled against Me" Notice the personal affront that YHWH feels! It is
not just the violation of His covenant, but the rebellion against Him, Him as husband, Him as King, Him
as the only God! Possibly Jer. 5:20-29 describes the attitude best.

The VERB "rebelled" (BDB 598, KB 632, Qal PERFECT) is
also found in Jer. 5:23; Lam. 1:18,20 (twice); and 3:42. However a SYNONYM (BDB 833, KB 981)
is used in Jer. 2:8,29; 3:13; 33:8; Lam. 3:42.

4:18 The invasion, destruction, and exile of the covenant people from the covenant land and the special
covenant city was their own fault. YHWH gave them only what they had sown (cf. Job 34:11; Ps. 28:4; 62:12;
Prov. 24:12; Eccl. 12:14; Jer. 17:10; 32:19; Matt. 16:27; 25:31-46; Rom. 2:6; 14:12; 1 Cor. 3:8; 2 Cor. 5:10; Gal. 6:7-10;
2 Tim. 4:14; 1 Pet. 1:17; Rev. 2:23; 20:12; 22:12). For a full list, see Gal. 6:7-10.

▣ "How bitter" This is the result of their rebellion (cf. Jer. 2:19; Amos 8:10). Note
Job 20:11-16; sin tastes good initially but becomes poison and brings death!

Their idolatry had spread into their very being (i.e. heart). They were sinful through
and through!

"My belly, my belly!"

Peshitta
"I am in pain! I am in pain!"

The MT has a NOUN (BDB 588) which means "bowels" or "inner parts" (cf.
NIDOTTE, vol. 2, pp. 1012-1013). Here it is parallel with "heart," which is another way of referring
to the place of feelings. The ancient Hebrews thought the seat of the emotions was in the lower viscera
(BDB 589 #5). This verse is emphasizing the terrible pain of Jeremiah's feelings about YHWH's coming judgment.

The VERB in v. 19 could come from

- חול ‒ BDB 296, KB 297, Qal COHORTATIVE, "writhe"

- יחל ‒ BDB 403 KB 407, Hiphil COHORTATIVE, "wait"

This information is from OT Parsing Guide (revised) by Beall, Banks, and Smith,
p. 546. The UBS Text Project and AB do not even mention the option.

▣ "The sound of the trumpet" The JPSOA notes that the MT has "you, O my being, hear," but
by a change of vocalization, yields, "I hear the blare of horns, my inner being, alarms of war" (p. 931).

4:20 "Disaster on disaster" The NOUN (BDB 991) is repeated for emphasis. This same
literary technique was used by isaiah.

Also notice that "devastated" (BDB 994) is also repeated in this verse (v. 30). Both of these similar
roots (שׁדד and שׁדר) are used often in Jeremiah.

▣ "tents. . .curtains" The NET Bible (p. 1298) makes the comment that this verse could refer to

- the weakness of Judah's defenses

- the destruction of a person's home (using an ancient cultural imagery)

The UBS Handbook on Jeremiah (p. 137) suggests that "tents" and "curtain" could be a
reference to the temple in Jerusalem.

▣ "in an instant" This is parallel with "suddenly" (v. 20c). The phrase "in an instant" (רגע, BDB 921), with
revocalization, can be translated "torn to shreds" (cf. LXX, NEB). This would fit the parallelism as well.

▣ "my. . .My" Apparently, Jeremiah is speaking as a Judean citizen. He is identifying with his people's plight!

4:21 The "standard" and "the trumpet" are military signaling devises, here of the invaders
(cf. Jer. 4:19).

The two VERBS of this verse are

- see ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERFECT used in a
COHORTATIVE sense

- hear ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal COHORTATIVE

4:22 This verse shows God's disappointment in His covenant people in strong images of irony.

- they are foolish (BDB 17)

- they do not know Me (BDB 393, KB 390, Qal PERFECT)

- they are stupid (BDB 698) children (cf. Isa. 1:2-3)

- they have no understanding (BDB 106, KB 122, Niphal PARTICIPLE)

- they are shrewd to do evil (BDB 314)

- they do not know how to do good (BDB 405, KB 408, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)

Notice how they are described in Jer. 5:21.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: JEREMIAH 4:23-26

23I looked on the earth, and behold, it was formless and void;

And to the heavens, and they had no light.

24I looked on the mountains, and behold, they were quaking,

And all the hills moved to and fro.

25I looked, and behold, there was no man,

And all the birds of the heavens had fled.

26I looked, and behold, the fruitful land was a wilderness,

And all its cities were pulled down

Before the Lord, before His fierce anger.

4:23-26 This strophe uses original creation in its chaotic state (i.e. "formless and void,"
cf. Gen. 1:2; "the heavens, and they had no light" before Gen. 1:3) to describe the destruction caused by
foreign (Mesopotamian) invasion.

As creation was originally without human habitation, so now the Promised Land is
without human habitation. This is not to be taken literally; there were always some Israelites and
Judeans not taken captive, but the land looked/seemed empty! (cf. Jer. 4:27).

Also notice the literary structure of "I looked. . ." (BDB 55, KB 65, Qal
PERFECT) used four times.

4:25 "all the birds of the heavens had fled" This may refer to the fact that even the carnivorous
birds have left because there is no more food (i.e. those killed in battle or invasion). Exile had emptied the land.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)

4:28 This verse speaks of the determined judgment of God (cf. Jer. 23:20; 30:24; Num. 23:19). There
is a greater purpose in the discipline of His covenant people (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN).
His discipline, in reality, was a sign of His parental love. He would not let them continue in their waywardness (i.e. Heb. 12:5-13).

Verse 28 personifies YHWH's creation (i.e. earth and heaven).

- The first two created things mourn over the coming judgment of Palestine, and especially of Jerusalem
and the temple (possibly Jer. 4:20c and d).

- The earth convulses as YHWH approaches (for blessing or judgment), cf. Rom. 8:18-22.

▣ "Because I have spoken" This alludes to the power of YHWH's word (cf. Isa. 55:9-11).

- I have spoken

- I have purposed

- I will not change My mind

- I will not turn from it

Judah reaped the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 after repeated warnings.

4:29 This verse describes what happened when an invading army swept across the land, and smaller
unwalled cities were defenseless and had to abandon their homes and shops. They tried to hide or seek
the shelter of a walled city.

4:30 This is an allusion to Judah as a harlot. Her lovers are the foreign powers with whom she
makes political alliances.

- dress in scarlet (BDB 1040)

- use gold ornaments (BDB 725 CONSTRUCT BDB 262)

- used dark highlighter around your eyes (i.e. with antimony)

This may reflect signs of wealth and social standing or characteristic signs of a prostitute. The
second option, in context, seems best. Political alliances were considered "spiritual/political adultery."

4:31 This allusion switches to birth pains (cf. Jer. 4:31; 6:24; 13:21; 22:23; 50:43). Not to bring
forth life, but death (cf. v. 30 f,g)! Judah's idolatry and covenant breaking have resulted in destruction, death, and exile!
